objective: Use a CHECK constraint to enforce a value rule at the database level.

original.hint: The word 'constraint' is the clue. Ask what the database can be made to refuse on your behalf.

objective: Distinguish NULL (absent/unknown) from 0, empty string and false.

original.hint: Ask why SQL needs IS NULL instead of letting you test the column with = 0 or = '' like any other value.
original.question: What does NULL represent?
options: The absence of a value (unknown/not applicable)
original.explanation: NULL marks a value that is missing or unknown, so it is not 0, not '' and not false, all of which are known values you can compare and index on. Because it is unknown, any comparison with it returns unknown rather than true, which is why WHERE col = NULL matches nothing and IS NULL exists. The same rule explains why COUNT(col) skips NULLs while COUNT(*) counts the rows.

defects: Correct option was conspicuously longer or more detailed than the alternatives.
rationale: Specify PostgreSQL and replace the any-comparison overstatement with ordinary equality and explicit NULL-aware predicates. Keep missing distinct from zero/empty/false.

objective: Justify TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE over a naive timestamp as recording an unambiguous instant.

original.hint: Ask what a stored value means when the writer and the reader sit in different time zones.
original.question: A TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE column is preferable to a naive timestamp because:
options: It records an unambiguous instant regardless of server time zone
original.explanation: In PostgreSQL, timestamptz converts the input to an absolute instant on write (stored as UTC) and renders it in the session time zone on read, so the same moment means the same thing to every server and client. A plain timestamp stores wall-clock digits with no zone, so a value like 2026-03-29 02:30 can be ambiguous or nonexistent depending on where it was written. Both types occupy 8 bytes and index identically, so storage and index speed are not the reason to pick one, and neither type says anything about NULL.

defects: Correct option was conspicuously longer or more detailed than the alternatives.
rationale: Limit the preference to event instants with known offsets. Remove universal index-speed claims and avoid suggesting that timestamptz can disambiguate an unspecified local wall time automatically.
evidence: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/datatype-datetime.html

objective: Identify the CAP conflict between availability during partition and linearizable read/write consistency.

original.hint: The choice only exists while the two sides cannot reach each other.
original.question: Under CAP, a distributed database that keeps accepting writes on both sides of a network partition has chosen:
options: Availability over consistency, with the replicas converging afterward
original.explanation: CAP describes what a system does during a partition: either it refuses requests on the side that cannot confirm the current state (CP) or it answers anyway and reconciles later (AP). Accepting writes on both sides means the replicas can disagree until they converge, which is what eventual consistency means. Durability is not part of the trade — both kinds still persist what they accept — and partition tolerance is not optional for anything spanning machines. Do not reduce this to 'SQL is CP, NoSQL is AP': MongoDB replica sets elect one primary and refuse writes on the minority side, while Cassandra and DynamoDB default to the availability side.

defects: Correct option was conspicuously longer or more detailed than the alternatives.
rationale: Specify both reads and writes on one replicated value, rather than inferring full CAP availability from write acceptance alone. Remove the unsupported convergence guarantee and product-default claims.
evidence: https://groups.csail.mit.edu/tds/papers/Gilbert/Brewer6.pdf
